title: Manage people-related security across the relationship lifecycle
summary: Personnel security applies proportionate controls from candidate screening through onboarding, role change, offboarding, and third-party engagement so that access, obligations, and accountability match a current business relationship.
outcome: Recommend the lifecycle control that best addresses a personnel or contractor security gap.
managerMindset: People controls should be consistent, lawful, proportionate, and connected to access and asset processes. Treat a transfer or contractor end date as a security event, not just an HR record change.

sections.title: Security follows the relationship
sections.body: Screening, job descriptions, agreements, orientation, supervision, transfer controls, and termination procedures each address a different lifecycle risk. The organization should define responsibilities, acceptable-use and confidentiality obligations, access approval, return of assets, and timely revocation. Controls must respect law, contracts, privacy, and the role’s actual risk rather than applying an arbitrary one-size-fits-all process.
keyPoints: A transfer requires removal as well as new access.
Offboarding must account for accounts, devices, credentials, knowledge transfer, and assets.

sections.title: Extend controls to nonemployees
sections.body: Vendors, consultants, and contractors may hold data, administer systems, or enter facilities without being employees. Agreements should define scope, security requirements, confidentiality, reporting, monitoring, access lifecycle, subcontracting conditions, and exit obligations. A business sponsor and service owner need to remain accountable for the relationship; procurement alone cannot operate the security control.
keyPoints: Contract language must be supported by onboarding, monitoring, and offboarding practice.
Third-party access is a lifecycle, not a permanent badge.

sections.title: Apply personnel controls across employee and third-party lifecycles
sections.body: Candidate screening and hiring should be proportional, authorized, consistent, and tied to role sensitivity. Employment agreements and policy-driven requirements establish confidentiality, acceptable use, intellectual-property, reporting, and sanctions expectations. Onboarding, transfer, and termination processes must create, change, review, or remove access, assets, duties, training, and acknowledgements promptly. Vendor, consultant, and contractor agreements must define scope, access, supervision, confidentiality, return or destruction, incident notice, and offboarding. Failure modes include orphaned access, unacknowledged obligations, bypassed screening, and suppliers treated as employees without equivalent contractual controls.
keyPoints: Name the accountable owner, decision criterion, and evidence for each applicable outline topic.
Record the failure consequence and escalation or review trigger rather than assuming a policy label proves operation.

sections.title: Apply personnel controls under local authority and role risk
sections.body: Personnel screening, agreements, monitoring, sanctions, and offboarding must be authorized, consistent, proportionate to the role, and aligned with labor, privacy, contract, and anti-discrimination obligations. Define the role sensitivity, permitted screening/monitoring basis, decision owner, evidence minimization and retention, appeal/escalation route, and trigger for re-screening or access review. An employment agreement or acknowledgment establishes obligations such as confidentiality, acceptable use, intellectual property, reporting, and sanctions only when it is valid and communicated under the applicable regime. Over-collection, inconsistent screening, or using an agreement as a substitute for access lifecycle controls creates legal, privacy, and security failures.
keyPoints: Risk-sensitive roles may justify stronger controls, but not an unlimited right to collect or monitor.
Keep personnel evidence limited to the authorized purpose and retention period.
A signed agreement does not itself revoke access or return assets at transfer or termination.

workedExamples.title: Clinical-to-procurement transfer
workedExamples.situation: An employee moves departments and gains new purchasing duties while retaining a clinical role.
workedExamples.reasoning: Trigger a role-change review, remove obsolete clinical privileges, grant the approved purchasing baseline, evaluate separation-of-duties conflicts, and retain evidence of the decision.
workedExamples.takeaway: The identity persists, but access must follow the current relationship.

workedExamples.title: Privileged contractor onboarding
workedExamples.situation: A contractor will administer a production identity service for six months.
workedExamples.reasoning: The sponsor defines privileged duties and required screening/contract clauses with HR, procurement, privacy, and counsel as applicable. Before access, verify the authorized engagement, confidentiality and acceptable-use terms, identity, role-based approvals, training, sponsor, expiry date, monitoring rules, and return/offboarding plan. Revalidate at renewal and remove access when work ends.
workedExamples.takeaway: A privileged relationship is a time-bounded, accountable lifecycle rather than a permanent account.

distinctions.difference: Personnel security governs lifecycle conditions and accountability; awareness develops behavior and understanding. Both are needed.
Role-proportionate screening is justified by documented duties and lawful authority; blanket screening applies the same collection regardless of need and may be unlawful or excessive.

misconceptions.claim: An HR termination record automatically ends all access.
misconceptions.correction: Technical and physical access, sessions, keys, supplier accounts, and assets require coordinated revocation and verification.

misconceptions.claim: A signed confidentiality agreement is enough personnel security.
misconceptions.correction: Agreements state obligations; security still needs authorized screening, onboarding, access review, supervision, transfer/offboarding controls, and evidence.

recallChecks.prompt: Why is a transfer a security event?
recallChecks.answer: The business need and authorized access change; old privileges may create excess access or conflicts.

recallChecks.prompt: What turns a supplier security clause into an operating control?
recallChecks.answer: An accountable owner plus onboarding, minimum requirements, monitoring, evidence, and controlled exit.

recallChecks.prompt: What must be established before collecting or retaining personnel-screening information?
recallChecks.answer: The role-risk rationale, lawful/contractual authority, purpose, decision owner, minimum information, retention, access restrictions, and escalation route.

scenarioSeeds.prompt: A contractor’s engagement ends Friday, but the account is reviewed only monthly. Which change most directly reduces exposure?
scenarioSeeds.decisiveDetail: The authoritative end event precedes the periodic review.

scenarioSeeds.prompt: A manager asks for the same intrusive screening for a low-risk temporary role and a privileged administrator role. What distinguishes the defensible decision?
scenarioSeeds.decisiveDetail: The documented role sensitivity, authorized purpose, proportionality, local legal/privacy constraints, and access consequences—not managerial preference alone.

studyPlan.learn: Map joiner, mover, leaver, and contractor events to control actions.
studyPlan.connect: Connect lifecycle events to Domain 5 provisioning and Domain 7 operations.
studyPlan.apply: List what must be revoked or verified after a contractor leaves.
studyPlan.revisit: In three days, explain why access review is not a substitute for event-driven offboarding.

visualLearningContract.teachingQuestion: Which lifecycle event changes access, evidence, or contractual control for this person or contractor?
visualLearningContract.misconception: Screening or an account disable completes personnel security.
visualLearningContract.formRationale: Aligned rows expose distinctions, decision criteria, and misuse consequences.
visualLearningContract.focalInsight: Lifecycle events require proportionate, attributable approvals and verified revocation across downstream paths.
visualLearningContract.intentionalOmissions: Detailed vendor commands and environment-specific parameters remain in the cited sources and are not implied by this learning view.
visualLearningContract.retrievalPrompt: For a mover, leaver, or contractor, state owner, access change, evidence, and completion check.
